extracted.intended_audience: young readers / readers of didactic Victorian moral fiction
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt of Victorian-era didactic children's fiction that models moral lessons and social expectations for young people (duties, temperance, education, humility, patience). Useful for studying or producing moralizing juvenile fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep from all appearance of evil (1 Thess. v.22)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a verse in the Bible which says we are to keep 'from all appearance of evil'. I was reading the chapter to mother last night, and she explained it to me as meaning that it is not enough for us to feel in our hearts that we do not mean wrong,—we must so act that there can be no mistake about our motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Act so that others cannot mistake your motives; outward behaviour must match inward convictions; avoid situations that create the appearance of wrongdoing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boldly do what is right regardless of consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: We must boldly do what we know to be right, regardless of consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not allow fear of ridicule or adverse consequences to prevent morally correct action; moral courage is a virtue to cultivate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confess faith openly; do not be ashamed
rubrics_metrics.description: Our Saviour says we are not to be ashamed of confessing Him before men; and when you let your brother's laughter make you stop singing your hymn, it would seem to him as if you were really ashamed of showing that you loved our Saviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain public expressions of conviction when appropriate; avoid yielding to peer pressure that conceals religious or moral commitments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value education over money
rubrics_metrics.description: In these days, education is better than money to a young man; for with a head well-stocked with useful knowledge, he is sure, so long as he conducts himself well, to go ahead in life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise learning and self-improvement over immediate financial gain; education is framed as a long-term investment in social mobility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use spare time productively; avoid idleness
rubrics_metrics.description: Time is a precious gift, lad, and one for the use or misuse of which God will call us all one day to give an account... one of the first [devices of Satan] is the tempting them to idle away their time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make good use of leisure hours (e.g., evening school); idle time is presented as a risk factor for moral decay and temptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid public-houses and temperance
rubrics_metrics.description: She says also that beer and spirits are really necessary to no one, and that at least a fourth part of the earnings of every working man who drinks beer are spent in the public-house.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temperance and avoidance of pubs are recommended on moral and economic grounds; money spent on drink is framed as lost opportunities for family welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid environments that facilitate bad habits
rubrics_metrics.description: It is so easy for young people to learn a bad habit, and so difficult to un-learn it; and therefore I have promised her never to go into such places as 'The Plough,' for fear of being tempted to do what it might afterwards be so hard to leave off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove yourself from places and company likely to encourage vice; preventive avoidance is better than attempting reformation later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against pride in knowledge; cultivate humility
rubrics_metrics.description: We must guard against pride of self-conceit in our knowledge. It is quite right to resolve... to improve our talents to the very utmost, and to employ them to the best advantage; but the motive throughout all should be, not an over-anxiety to appear more clever than other people, or to obtain the praise of men for our superior knowledge; but rather how we shall best be fulfilling God's will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motives for self-improvement should be humble and service-oriented rather than self-aggrandising; humility is an ethical constraint on ambition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do your duty to your master; be conscientious at work
rubrics_metrics.description: Do your duty strictly to your master; bear no ill-will towards any one; seek for no revenge... 'Your evening studies must not interfere with your duty to me, remember.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance education with obligations; demonstrate reliability, carefulness (e.g., putting tools away), and steady conduct to earn trust and advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bear unjust suspicions meekly and patiently
rubrics_metrics.description: If our blessed Saviour, 'who did no sin,' suffered unjustly, we should think it no strange thing that we should; and knowing how patiently and meekly He bore insult and wrong, we should pray for His Spirit to enable us to do so also.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond to false accusations with patience and without seeking revenge; emulate Christ-like meekness when wronged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek no revenge; pray for enemies
rubrics_metrics.description: Bear no ill-will towards any one; seek for no revenge, even if you come to be certain of the justice of your suspicions... 'Pray for them that despitefully use you and persecute you.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transform hostility into intercessory prayer; moral instruction emphasises forgiveness and active compassion rather than retaliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small acts of influence matter
rubrics_metrics.description: As in the old fable, the efforts of a tiny mouse were of service in setting free a great lion, so even young people have it in their power to help forward great and important results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage young people to take advantage of opportunities to influence others; modest actions can have large effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching for children: be brief, simple, and entertaining
rubrics_metrics.description: I shall not call it a lecture... as it will not last more than a quarter of an hour... I shall call it, then, a pleasant talk... I think that if I take a number of great and interesting facts out of some of those books, and tell them to you in simple language, such as even the youngest amongst you will be able to understand, it may give you a little stock of useful general knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When informing young learners: avoid long dry discourse, keep talks short, use simple language, select interesting facts, invite questions, and aim to entertain as well as instruct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be ready to help one another; kindness as duty
rubrics_metrics.description: We should always be ready to help one another... You are a good-natured fellow... We all have opportunities, at some time or another, of influencing a companion, either by his advice or example. Take advantage of every such occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Altruism and mutual aid are moral duties; practical kindness (even at personal inconvenience) is praised and modelled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate competence to gain trust and advancement
rubrics_metrics.description: You are a sharp lad, and a steady one too, and will rise in the world, if I am not very much mistaken... 'You are rather young to be trusted with such work as that; but you seem to know what you are about.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skill, steadiness, and attention to detail at work lead to trust from superiors and greater opportunities; craftsmanship and exactness are virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intercessory prayer cultivates charity
rubrics_metrics.description: No one can pray for his enemies and not feel kindly towards them... The very act of praying for another is unselfish in itself; and it is impossible to feel anger and bitterness towards one for whom we are asking God's grace and favour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages the practice of praying for those who wrong you as a means to overcome resentment and increase personal charity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid questionable companions who exert coercive influence
rubrics_metrics.description: There was something in Tom Haines' manner to Frank which struck Walter particularly. It seemed to the boy as if Tom felt that he had Frank in his power in some way or other, and could make any use of him he liked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of friends who dominate or manipulate you; choose companions whose influence is positive and not coercive.
